topic: What the Guide is and its terms

notes.front: In the Guide’s own conventions, what does the word “Kanban” mean?
notes.back: The whole set of concepts in the Guide, specifically as they apply to knowledge work.
notes.explanation: The Guide sets this convention so the word points to its own concepts. It is scoped to knowledge work: work whose main input is people’s knowledge and expertise, by people who think for a living, such as in software, analysis or finance.
notes.example: A software team, a finance team and a hospital planning team can all apply Kanban in this sense to their knowledge work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Conventions Used”, p. 2; Wikipedia, “Knowledge worker” (lead section)

notes.front: What is The Kanban Guide, and what does it aim to be?
notes.back: A short document by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti. It aims to be a unifying reference offering the minimal guidance for Kanban.
notes.explanation: “Minimal” is deliberate: the Preface says various approaches can complement Kanban, depending on the context. This deck follows the May 2025 edition.
notes.example: Like a rulebook that fixes only the essentials of a game and leaves the tactics to the players.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Preface”, p. 2; authors as named on p. 1 of the kanbanguides.org edition 2025.5

notes.front: In the Guide’s conventions, what does “Kanban system” mean?
notes.back: The same as “Kanban”: the whole set of the Guide’s concepts, as they apply to knowledge work.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines “Kanban or Kanban system” in a single convention, so both names refer to the same set of concepts.
notes.example: “Our Kanban system” means the team’s whole way of applying these concepts, not just a chart on the wall.

notes.front: What is a stakeholder, in the Guide’s conventions?
notes.back: An entity, individual or group responsible for, interested in, or affected by the inputs, activities and outcomes of the Kanban system.
notes.explanation: Stakeholders matter because the Guide defines value as a benefit for a stakeholder.
notes.example: For a team building a payroll app: the client paying for it, the staff who are paid through it and the tax office all count.

notes.front: What is value, in the Guide’s conventions?
notes.back: Either a potential or a realized benefit for a stakeholder.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s examples include meeting the needs of the customer, the end-user, the organization and the environment, so value is broader than money.
notes.example: A feature not yet released is potential value; once people use it and benefit, the value is realized.

notes.front: What does “visualize” (or “visualization”) mean in the Guide’s conventions?
notes.back: Any method of conveying ideas effectively, including clarifying a concept; it is not necessarily visual.
notes.explanation: So when the Guide asks you to visualize something, a picture is one option, not a requirement.
notes.example: A spoken walkthrough of the team’s work for a colleague who cannot see a screen still counts as visualizing it.

notes.front: What is risk, in the Guide’s conventions?
notes.back: The chance that something bad could happen.
notes.explanation: The Guide says that, ultimately, Kanban’s strategy is to help you understand trade-offs and manage risk.
notes.example: The chance that an important item misses the date a customer needs it by.

notes.front: Who are Kanban system members?
notes.back: Those who participate in the value delivery of a Kanban system.
notes.explanation: Most of the Guide’s rules are addressed to them: they define their workflow, manage the work in it and improve it.
notes.example: The analysts, developers and testers who do and deliver a team’s work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Definition of Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: The Kanban Guide sets out to give only the {{c1::minimal}} guidance for Kanban, as a unifying reference for the community.
notes.explanation: It leaves room for other approaches to complement Kanban, depending on the context.

notes.front: According to the Guide’s Preface, what can complement Kanban?
notes.back: Various approaches, depending on the context, so that Kanban can accommodate the full range of value delivery and organizational challenges.
notes.explanation: The Guide keeps itself minimal on purpose and expects other approaches to sit alongside it.

notes.front: Are the Guide’s conventions meant to replace other definitions of the same terms?
notes.back: No. They clarify how the terms are intended to be applied in the Guide.
notes.explanation: The Preface says the conventions are not meant to replace any other existing definitions.

notes.front: The Guide’s conventions define Kanban (or Kanban system), stakeholder, value and visualize (or visualization). Which fifth term do they define?
notes.explanation: Five conventions in all; the Guide added them in 2025 “to convey intent”.

notes.front: As the Guide uses the word, Kanban concerns {{c1::knowledge work}} specifically.
notes.explanation: The convention for “Kanban or Kanban system” ends “specifically as pertains to knowledge work”.

notes.front: In the Guide, a benefit for a stakeholder counts as value whether it is {{c1::potential or realized}}.
notes.explanation: Value need not have been delivered yet: potential value counts too.

notes.front: A colleague says The Kanban Guide is a complete handbook that fixes every meeting, role and tool. Is that how the Guide describes itself?
notes.back: No. It offers the minimal guidance for Kanban and expects other approaches to complement it.
notes.explanation: The Preface calls it a unifying reference offering minimal guidance; the rest is left to context.

notes.front: An insurance team spends its days analysing claims and drafting policies. Is its work the kind the Guide’s definition of Kanban is aimed at?
notes.back: Yes. It is knowledge work, and the Guide names finance among the fields that have benefited.
notes.explanation: The Guide scopes Kanban to knowledge work and says its application is not limited to any specific industry.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Conventions Used”, p. 2; “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: A regulator never touches a team’s work but is affected by what the team delivers. Is the regulator a stakeholder in the Guide’s sense?
notes.back: Yes. Anyone affected by the Kanban system’s outcomes is a stakeholder.
notes.explanation: The convention covers anyone responsible for, interested in, or affected by the system’s inputs, activities or outcomes.

notes.front: A change cuts a product’s energy use, though no paying customer notices. Can this count as value under the Guide’s convention?
notes.back: Yes. Value is a benefit for a stakeholder, and the Guide’s examples include the environment.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists the customer, the end-user, the organization and the environment as examples of whose needs value can meet.

notes.front: A team records a spoken briefing that explains clearly how its work moves. Does that count as visualizing its work, in the Guide’s sense?
notes.back: Yes. The Guide’s convention covers any method that conveys ideas effectively, not only visual ones.
notes.explanation: “Visualize” in the Guide is not limited to pictures.

notes.front: Before a release, a team asks: “What is the chance this breaks the payment page?” Which of the Guide’s conventions is the question about?
notes.explanation: The Guide defines risk as the chance that something bad could happen.

notes.front: A finance director reads monthly reports on a team’s output but does no delivery work. Is the director a Kanban system member or a stakeholder?
notes.back: A stakeholder, not a Kanban system member: members are those who participate in value delivery.
notes.explanation: The director is interested in the outcomes, which makes them a stakeholder, but takes no part in delivering value.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Conventions Used”, p. 2; “Definition of Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What is the difference between a stakeholder and a Kanban system member?
notes.back: Members take part in delivering value. Stakeholders are anyone responsible for, interested in or affected by the system’s inputs, activities or outcomes.
notes.explanation: The two overlap but are not the same group: someone can be affected by a Kanban system without working in it.
notes.contrast: Stakeholder is about interest or effect; member is about participation in delivery.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Conventions Used”, p. 2; “Definition of Kanban”, p. 4
